A knave is a dishonest, deceitful, and cunning man — someone who tricks, cheats, or manipulates others for personal gain. Think of a swindler, a schemer, or a con artist. The key idea is not just that a knave is a bad person, but that he is specifically sneaky and untrustworthy. He lies, he plots, he deceives. He uses his cleverness not for good, but to take advantage of others.

If someone called you a knave, they would be saying: "You are a crafty, unscrupulous person who cannot be trusted."
What Makes a Knave Different From Other "Bad Guys"?

This is an important distinction. Not every bad person is a knave:

  • A brute is physically violent and aggressive. A knave doesn't need brute force — he uses deception and cunning instead.
  • A villain is broadly evil in a grand sense. A knave is more personal and sneaky.
  • A fool is simply stupid. A knave is actually quite clever — he just uses that cleverness dishonestly.
  • A rogue is the closest comparison and is often used interchangeably with knave, but "rogue" can sometimes be said almost affectionately (a lovable rogue), while "knave" is almost always meant as a genuine insult.

So the heart of the word is this: deliberate, scheming dishonesty. A knave knows what he is doing is wrong, and he does it anyway because it benefits him.

In a standard deck of playing cards, the Jack is also called the knave. This is the card that ranks between the Ten and the Queen in each suit (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades). This usage is old and somewhat formal, but it still appears — especially in British English and in classical card game literature. So if you ever read an old book that mentions "the knave of hearts," it simply means the Jack of Hearts.
The Older, Weaker Meaning (Now Rarely Used)

In very old usage (centuries ago), "knave" simply meant a male servant or a boy of low social class — with no necessary dishonesty implied. A kitchen knave, for example, was just a lowly kitchen worker. Over time, the word drifted away from this innocent meaning and picked up the strong negative sense of trickery and moral corruption that it has today. This older usage is essentially dead in modern English, and you will only encounter it in very old texts.
How the Word Is Used Today

"Knave" is not an everyday word in modern English. You are unlikely to hear it in casual conversation. However, you will encounter it regularly in:

  • Classic literature — especially Shakespeare, who used the word constantly. Iago in Othello, for example, is repeatedly called a knave — and rightly so, because he is the ultimate deceiver.
  • Historical novels and period dramas — set in medieval or early modern times, where the word fits the era.
  • Card game writing — where "knave" is used for the Jack.
  • Poetry and formal prose — where a writer wants a word that sounds sharp, old-fashioned, and cutting.

• "He is nothing but a knave — he smiled to my face while stealing from my purse."
  • "Beware of that merchant; every man in the village knows him to be a knave."
  • "The play's villain is a classic knave: charming on the outside, rotten to the core."
  • "She played the knave of spades and won the hand." (card game context)

• Knavery (noun): The behavior of a knave — acts of cheating, scheming, and dishonesty. "The court was shocked by the sheer knavery of the accused."
  • Knavish (adjective): Describing someone or something that has the qualities of a knave — sneaky, dishonest, crafty. "He gave a knavish smile before disappearing with the money."

These words share territory with "knave," so knowing them together helps you understand the word more fully:
scoundrel, rogue, rascal, trickster, schemer, swindler, cheat, villain.

A knave is a cunning, dishonest, and untrustworthy man who uses deceit and scheming to serve his own selfish ends — the kind of person you should never trust with your money, your secrets, or your back.
